Mr. Speaker, my constituency, the great riding of Moose Jaw, has the distinction of having the lowest priced gasoline of any constituency in Canada. Last weekend the price of regular gas in Davidson, Saskatchewan, was 38.6 cents per litre.
In spite of this price I feel that there are many unanswered questions in the industry, and gas prices should be much lower right across Canada. For example, why have we seen such a small reduction in the pump price of gasoline when world level crude oil prices have dropped so dramatically?
The middle man in this arrangement is the refiner. I, and many thousands of Canadians, would like to know why the refiners' price decrease has not been passed on to consumers.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN PRICE OF PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
REDUCTION IN PRICE OF PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we all know, the price of gas is following the drop in crude oil prices, for the greater benefit of the Canadian consumer. However, we cannot stop there. I think it is high time the big oil companies adjusted their stride and started cutting wholesale prices for heating oil and diesel fuel. When they do, the independents will be able to offer heating oil users a better price. It is now up to the big companies to show some respect for the small independents who often have to pay for this drop in prices out of their own money, in order to compete. I hope they will soon get the message and adjust their prices so that all consumers will be able to benefit from lower prices on diesel fuel and heating oil as well. It is time all Canadians were

subsubtopic: LACK OF APPLICANTS FOR BRICKLAYING JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the House to a catch-22 dilemma which Mr. Peter Zilli, the owner of Prill Construction in my riding, is facing. He is in dire need of 20 bricklayers. After nine months of repeated calls to Employment Canada, it has yet to meet the order. Employment and Immigration Canada cannot have it both ways. There must be greater efficiency and precision in the system, for companies like Prill Construction find themselves in a precarious and frustrating position. In the meantime I urge unemployed bricklayers to call my Toronto office at 743-3153.

subsubtopic: MEASURES ADVOCATED TO ASSIST AGRICULTURAL INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, agriculture is the historic root of the Canadian economy. We have what it takes-the land, advanced techniques, and excellent farmers. However, with all of this, the industry is in crisis. The Government of Canada recognizes this and has given agriculture a high priority on its agenda.
I want to offer three suggestions which 1 feel will help alleviate the problems faced by our farmers. The first is crop insurance. Crop insurance should provide coverage of real costs on a farm by farm basis. This would then cover disasters such as the recent drought. Second is commodity prices. The EEC and the U.S.A. Government must be persuaded to include agricultural commodities under GATT. This should eliminate the huge world surpluses caused by subsidies, and should result in higher prices. The third is domestic prices. We need to look at higher domestic prices on agricultural commodities in order to protect our agricultural industry and allow it to continue to be the base of the Canadian economy.

subtopic: QUOTAS ON CARS IMPORTED FROM CERTAIN COUNTRIES
QUOTAS ON CARS IMPORTED FROM CERTAIN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an unfair situation in this country that is affecting the automobile retail sector. More and more cars manufactured in so-called developing countries are imported without being subject to customs duty or to the import quotas set for cars imported from countries like Japan.
A Toyota dealer in my riding of Verdun-Saint-Paul is outraged at these discriminatory measures. He considers this to be unfair competiton, and he is right.
When some countries manage to sell nearly 80,000 cars a year in Canada at very competitive prices, it would make sense to put them on the same footing as industrialized countries and make them subject to the same customs tariff. We should also get rid of all import quotas on foreign cars in order to promote a free and competitive market that would certainly benefit the Canadian consumer.

The study showed that although there are almost two million children age 12 and under in Canada, there are only about 172,000 licensed child care spaces.

Mr. Speaker, just over one year ago the House gave unanimous consent to a motion that I introduced to have a statue of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker commissioned and placed on Parliament Hill. I am pleased to inform all Members that an artist has been chosen and that a maquette has now been completed.

ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-ENERGY-FALLING WORLD PRICES Mr. Russell MacLellan (Cape Breton-The Sydneys) moved:
That this House regrets that the Government's energy policy has proven to be disastrous for both the industry and the consumer in its failure to give the consumer the benefit of falling world energy prices and in its confusion and lack of direction, creating uncertainty for the oil and gas industry in the face of the Government's inability to cope with changing international conditions and its refusal to fulfil its commitments.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a shame that we had to move this motion, but the situation in the energy industry leaves us no alternative. It is becoming chaotic. The policy of the Government is benefiting no one, except perhaps the integrated oil
March 19, 1986

companies. The policy of the Government is not benefiting the consumer, the producer, or the independent retailer.
There were drastic price reductions in world oil in January. These reductions have not been passed on to the consumer at the pumps. There were two price declines at the pump which are not, in any sense of the word, adequate for the consumers of the country. Consumers are being gouged. The first price decline of 2 cents a litre was only at the pump and not in the wholesale price. Therefore, independent retailers had to take 2 cents a litre off their profit margin in order to remain competitive. Independent retailers did not benefit from this first price decline which came grudgingly from the industry at the reluctant urging of the Government. Through the policy of the Government independent retailers are being squeezed by the large integrated oil companies to the extent that they may not be able to remain in business.
At the forefront of this policy is Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada's wholesale price to retailers in the United States is 4 to 6 cents a litre cheaper than it is to retailers in Canada. The people's own oil company is selling gasoline in the United States cheaper at the wholesale level than it is selling it to its own retailers in Canada.
With regard to producers, all Canadian-produced crude used in domestic markets has been undervalued since early January of 1986 by between $4 and $6 Canadian a barrel. That is because the integrated oil companies switched from a west Texas intermediate posted price to a west Texas intermediate spot price. The lowest possible price which could be paid for crude oil in the world is being paid by Petro-Canada to producers in western Canada. This is tragic at this time while we are trying to safeguard and foster this industry in an attempt to keep together what we have achieved in this country in relation to production and security of supply.
Canadian producers are losing up to $6.6 million a day based on deliveries to domestic markets of 1.1 million barrels per day. The 1.1 million barrels per day produced in western Canada amounts to nearly 80 per cent of Canada's total crude consumption of 1.4 million barrels per day, the rest being sold as imports, mainly to the United States. This 1.1 million barrels per day represents 85 per cent of Canada's total crude production of 1.7 million barrels per day.
What is all this nonsense the Government has been telling us about prices not being able to go down until it flows through the system? Eighty per cent of our oil comes from western Canada and is refined in the country. Still, there have only been two measly reductions at the pump and consumers continue to be gouged by an artificially high price. Producers are being gouged by being paid the lowest price for crude oil in the world. This is being done by the people's own oil company, Petro-Canada.
The price is being kept artificially high. Petro-Canada has done nothing for prices. It has not led price declines in the country. The first price decline was 1 cent per litre by Imperial Oil. The next day Petro-Canada followed with a 2 cent a litre reduction. The second reduction at the pumps was announced jointly by Imperial Oil and Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada is
Supply
keeping the price of gasoline artificially high and it is being aided and abetted by the Government. The Government need only call the president of Petro-Canada and tell him to start acting in the interests of the Canadian consumer. The result of this is that in January alone Canadians paid $302 million too much at the pumps for gasoline. That does not include the extra which they paid for heating oil and other petroleum products.
The United States has not had this problem. Their prices went down at the pumps when world oil prices went down. The prices at the pumps in the United States reflected the price of world oil and the fact that refined gasoline is a separate commodity from crude oil, the same as crude oil is separate from pork bellies. In Canada we have had to listen to all this nonsense about a flow-through period which has just been a con of the Canadian people.
This is all because the Government is changing the role of Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada was set up to explore and develop energy sources in the country and to establish a security of supply on which we could rely. Petro-Canada is no longer doing this. In fact, it is backing out of five wells off the East Coast of Canada. It is reducing its exploration and development budget. It is no longer a window on the market for Canadians. Consumers cannot rely on Petro-Canada to act on their behalf at all. Petro-Canada is being told by the Government to make money at all costs, to drive up its profits in order to present the best possible picture so its shares will draw the best possible price at a private share sale. This is not in the interest of consumers, but in the interest of serving the policy of the Government, which policy is not in the interest of Canadian consumers.
The philosophy has changed with respect to Petro-Canada and the people of the country realize it. At one time Petro-Canada was a source of pride. We could buy from our own oil company and get a fair deal. People wanted to do that. Now they look upon Petro-Canada as a gouger, a monster out of control causing problems in the country which have never been experienced before, at both the producer and consumer levels. All of this has been exacerbated by the Government's policy with regard to Petro-Canada to do nothing to help the producer or the consumer. If the Government's policy was to act in the best interests of the industry and the consumer, we would not have these problems in the country at this time.
Not only did the Government change its policy to act against Canadians, it also purchased the down-stream assets, the refining and marketing capability, of what was once Gulf Canada in Ontario and western Canada. Now they have such a large number of stations they control the marketing industry. They have consumers by the throat. Not only that. There are hundreds of producers but only four major refineries. There are smaller companies with maybe one refinery, but just four major refineries. They pay producers the lowest price and then gouge the consumers.

March 19, 1986
Supply
What does all this mean? It means the Government has taken a good public-minded Crown corporation and turned it against Canadians. This party is diametrically opposed to using Petro-Canada to gouge the industry and consumer. Petro-Canada was set up for the benefit of the oil and gas industry as well as the consumer, not to act to their detriment.
Certainly the reduction in the price of oil will cause a reduction in oil exploration and development, the non-conventional sources in particular. It is not the industry that caused this cloud. It is the Government, through its jaundiced policies and crazed directions to Petro-Canada, which has caused the problem. It is the Government that backed away from the commitment to the Husky upgrader which was made by the former Government. Why? The Government says it is worried about world oil prices. It does not bother to consider for a minute the fact that when the upgrader is finished world oil prices will be higher. It does not consider for a minute that its own budget documents indicate the price of crude oil will be U.S. $22.50. Mind you, that is on page 23 of the document. On page 20 the Government says the price is going to be U.S. $23.88. On the one hand the Government says the price will average U.S. $22.50 this year, on the other hand it says it has to reconsider the Husky upgrader because of the price of oil. No wonder no one has any respect for this Government or its economic policies.
The Government is also applying retroactively regulations which have yet to be implemented under the Petroleum Incentives Program Act. As a result, Canadian companies, particularly Husky-Bow Valley, have been squeezed out of wells they wanted to drill on the east coast. Initially they wanted to drill 10 wells. The Government talked them into reducing that to seven. Then the Government, through the retroactive application of regulations which no one has seen officially, has reduced the number of wells to two. This is diabolical. The Government has also said that if Petro-Canada backs out of exploration it earned without cost through a back-in provision, the partner who replaces Petro-Canada will not receive funds under PIP for their interest.
Where are we going here? What is happening? Our energy policy is in shreds. Consumers are being taken advantage of completely, yet the Government is not moving. The industry even visited the Government yesterday to explain the dire situation facing them throughout Canada. The Government would not listen. The Minister is frozen to her deregulation switch. She is going to hold on for dear life. The industry is going to suffer regardless.
What is happening to the industry, and by that I mean primarily the small and medium oil companies? They are in a tremendously difficult position, teetering on the brink, because of the policies of this Government. They are ripe for bankruptcy or takeover by the multinational oil companies. They have proven reserves of oil and gas. The large oil companies are able to withstand this bad time because of their integrated nature. They realize the small companies are vulnerable, and if they wait until they become even more vulnerable they can pick up
their reserves for practically nothing. They can steal it out from underneath this country. That is a tragedy. Yet, how can you blame them?
The Government is saying to its own Crown corporation: You do the same thing. Petro-Canada led the price increases last fall but did not lead the price decreases this spring. The multinationals have a shield; they just follow behind Petro-Canada's gouging and they are safe from criticism because Petro-Canada is leading the way.
What is going to happen? Producers presently receive a rebate of 75 per cent of royalties due, up to $3 million. That is a provincial responsibility. Similarly, they are exempt from the PGRT up to the first $500,000. At the current rate of 10 per cent that means $5 million worth of oil and gas production is exempt. The Government should consider increasing this threshold in order to protect the small and medium producer. It should use this policy as a lever to force the producing provinces to reduce their royalties. It has to be done. This Government has to move because everyone is suffering; everyone except the integrated oil companies. This is tragic. There has never been such an injustice in Canadian commerce like the one being perpetrated by this Government. The time to review the policy is not in five months, the time is now. The Government has to act now on behalf of the industry and consumers. We should not sell our oil and gas to foreign countries for less than we pay for it in Canada. That is not commerce in the interests of the Canadian public. The consumer deserves better from this Government. The industry, which put faith in the Government, deserves much better.
Are there questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I did not hear the Hon. Member correctly. He suggested that the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax, which is a tax imposed on the industry and which will be phased out by the Government, will give a dramatic increase in revenues to the oil industry. 1 believe he said it had a threshold of $500,000 in terms of income and that the smaller companies do not have to pay this tax right now. He suggested that the threshold should be increased. In other words, smaller oil companies should not have to pay the tax.
This is a big issue right now. The Canadian Petroleum Association, the voice of big oil, has been pushing for the elimination of the PGRT. I know that such a move will benefit the big oil companies since they are the ones paying the tax. I think the Hon. Member has quite correctly pointed out that some small oil companies do not have to pay this tax while others which are small but not the smallest have to pay some. To what would the Hon. Member increase the threshold?

Mr. Speaker, that is a very good question posed by my friend, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I do not have a particular figure since 1 have not had an opportunity to thoroughly investigate the
March 19, 1986

matter. However, I will be having meetings next week with the express purpose of finding out exactly what threshold could best service the industry in order to protect Canadian companies which are now just hanging on by their fingernails.

We in the New Democratic Party do not believe that the PGRT should be eliminated with respect to provincial royalties. We feel that is a provincial matter. The pressure is coming from the big oil companies which will be able to survive no matter to what level oil prices drop. They are integrated companies with a great number of assets. They will be able to ride out the storm. It is the small Canadian companies which are in real danger. As the Hon. Member has pointed out this may result in the elimination of the Canadian industry completely. It is the perfect time for big multinational oil companies to take over small Canadian companies.
What is the Hon. Member's position and that of his Party with respect to a floor price for oil, or with respect to a negotiated price for oil? I have always believed that the real problem has been created by the ups and downs. As a westerner, Mr. Speaker, you know about the boom-and-bust syndrome in Alberta. That most recent boom lasted only about three to six months. It seems to me that the bust part of the syndrome is now coming on. I would like to see this situation levelled out so that we can have continued growth in western Canada.
Do members of the Liberal Party believe that there should be some sort of negotiated price if the price of oil keeps dropping dramatically? It seems to me that getting rid of the PGRT would allow better benefits to flow to small Canadian companies. In other words, they would receive a livable price for their oil and they would not have to sell it all out now at fire-sale prices.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to correct my hon. friend. I do not think he meant to say that we advocate doing away with the PGRT. What we are saying is that the threshold of $5 million should be raised in order to allow small and medium-sized Canadian companies to gain more benefits and relief from the PGRT. However, that would have to be linked to a commitment from the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in order to reduce the royalties so that a further benefit could accrue. There is certainly no need to do away with the PGRT, as far as I can see, since it would be allowed to move into higher amounts. It would only affect the larger corporations which I feel are better able to weather the storm. At least that is the way it looks to me right now.
With respect to a floor price, the Liberal Party is not prepared to advocate the setting of a floor price at the present time. No one from the industry has come to my Party requesting that a floor price be set. We are not about to go out to the industry and suggest that a floor price be put in place when no one in the industry has come to us asking for such a price. Why would we do that? If we were to do that we would be saying to consumers that they will have to pay higher prices for gasoline while we are advocating that the price come down. We would be saying that consumers get the benefit of the world price reduction in crude oil. We would also be saying to
Supply
the business community, the manufacturers and the industries that they will have to pay more for oil for industrial purposes. This would be like saying to these groups that they must place themselves at a disadvantage with respect to competitors in other countries. We have not been asked to advocate a floor price. We see a definite downside to the imposition of such a price. We are certainly not advocating a floor price at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to what the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) had to say. He talked about raising the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax credit to a figure above $500,000. However, he did not have a specific figure in this respect. Perhaps the Hon. Member can tell us from where this money would come. Would there be some sort of a dip into the Treasury? Is the Hon. Member proposing to raise the debt?

Mr. Speaker, it would give me great pleasure to address the Hon. Member's question. There will be nothing more serious to the country than the loss of our oil and gas industry. I think there is a definite possibility that we will lose it. I think we are being very kind to the Saudi Arabians and other countries. Not only does price reduction mean that these countries will be able to compete with other producers, it means that conservation will be relaxed while consumption will be increased. It will also mean that synthetic oil projects will no longer be economically viable. We must be mindful of these points. We cannot throw away everything that we have worked for in light of the policies of this Government and the former Liberal Government. I refer to the Government's goal to achieve self-sufficiency and Canadianization. That cannot be thrown away.
If the Hon. Member is worried about the cost, and of course there is a relationship with respect to what will be most harmful to the country, then I say to him: Go to the industry and tell it we will relax this measure now but when prices increase again they will have to pay it back to the Government of Canada. That is perfectly fine with me, if that is what the Hon. Member wants to do.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to make some comments on behalf of my Party. 1 will not speak extensively on this matter.
I wish to say that we are in a crisis situation. Canadians should not be smug, thinking of it as being just an Albertan problem because it is a Canadian problem as well. It is somewhat ironic that we are in a crisis when oil prices increase dramatically and that we are in a crisis when oil prices decrease dramatically. As I said before, that is all part of the boom-and-bust syndrome. This syndrome is incorporated into the Western Accord as we follow world prices. It is a situation we have to get out of in Canada. It is not doing the country any good, and it could devastate Alberta. Right now Alberta is like the Titanic. It has a big hole in the side as a result of lower world oil prices. The lifeboats and preservers have been thrown overboard. The Province does not want to use them because of ideological grounds. The party is still going on.

Well, it has to come to an end at least. Perhaps that is somewhat unfair. Perhaps the party is grinding to a halt because of this recognition. We could face up to 40 per cent unemployment in Alberta if oil prices continue to drop. I saw the news at 11:30 this morning with respect to OPEC oil prices and they may, in fact, be stabilized now somewhat. However, I believe that is very doubtful because we are not sure what will happen. My Party believes that the way to protect the Alberta producer is to establish a temporary floor price until the market stabilizes.
The Minister accused us of living in a fantasy world because I and others have been leading advocates in the House for lowering the prices at the pumps. However, I suggest that is a different matter. The reason we are not seeing lower oil prices at the pumps is that our system is not competitive. There are a few companies, including Petro-Canada, that control the market and they are simply not quickly passing on the dramatically lower oil prices. In fact, at a time when the price at the pumps should be reduced by 10 cents a litre, these companies are creaming off profits.
The fact is that it could be a matter of Government policy to lower the prices at the pumps in order to benefit consumers, while being stabilized at the small producer level. However, nothing is being done and we are getting the worst of all possible worlds as a result of the so-called free market economy.
I was in Alberta and met with some small producers. They will be devastated by what is taking place in the Province of Alberta. Husky Oil, Petro-Canada, Suncor, Syncrude, Canadian Roxy, Sulpetro and Pembica Resources have formally announced lay-offs or staff cut-backs totalling 1,500. Ipso, the Regina-based steel maker, will eliminate 695 workers. The Canadian Association of Oilwell Drill Contractors predicts that 4,000 jobs will vanish in that sector this spring. Dome Petroleum has informed its bankers that it has no intention of making payments on its massive debt of $5.2 billion. We could face another banking crisis if Dome Petroleum goes under. The President of the 30,000 strong Petroleum Services Association says that the total job loss in that sector this year will be 6,000 and could go as high as 15,000.
The Alberta Energy Board has chopped the provincial allowable daily input by 300,000 barrels a day, which is approximately one-third of total production. One oil man is quoted as saying that it is Armageddon in Alberta and that every major oil project is threatened. Clearly there are problems in Alberta which we must address and I will make some suggestions about how we can deal with those problems.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) stated that the Government's energy policy is in tatters. Originally, the federal Government's energy policy was to get rid of the National Energy Program, go to world oil market prices and phase out the petroleum and gas revenue tax which provided a lot of money to the federal Government. The oil companies despised the PGRT because they had to pay
tax for once. The Government's move to world oil prices gave the oil industry another windfall since it increased the price of their old oil which they obtained at very low rates. The oil industry was to become the engine of economic growth that would create 300,000 new jobs in Canada and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) stated that this would be the Government's major economic policy.
In March or April of 1985 the Government entered into the Western Accord with the oil producing provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan in western Canada. What has become of the Government's energy policy? It is in tatters because the price of oil has fallen dramatically in the so-called free market which is essentially controlled by OPEC. The result has been the lay-offs and cut-backs which 1 have just mentioned.
Now, the Government has changed its policy. The Minister of Finance has announced a new policy of consumer-led economic growth because of lower oil prices at the pumps. While that may be a legitimate policy, the Government has made a 180 degree turn from its original energy policy. I challenge the Government to tell me that it has not changed its policy. Furthermore, the Minister has not even been honest in explaining this policy. His Budget estimates the price of oil to be $22.50 a barrel for the rest of 1986 and he projected revenues according to that figure. Therefore, he has underestimated his deficit by $2 billion in order to bring the deficit under that magic figure of $30 billion.
The Government's original policy was to rely on the oil industry as the engine of economic growth, but its present policy is to rely on consumer-led recovery and growth through lower oil prices. While that may be a commendable policy, it is a complete change from its original energy policy.
The Government has created the worst of all possible worlds because the oil industry is suffering in Alberta and the consumer is not getting justice at the pump. Our system is so non-competitive that those lower prices have not been passed on to consumers, yet the Government has done nothing to make the system more competitive. In fact, it has closed a refinery in Montreal.
I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources why oil prices were not 6 cents a litre lower. I even introduced a motion in the House stating that the price at the pump should be 6 cents a litre lower. When I suggested that gasoline prices were cheaper in California and other states directly across the border, the Minister replied that our system is different from that in the United States. She explained that we do not have the refining capacity that exists in California, yet the Government has closed a refinery in Montreal.
I suggested that Petro-Canada could be used to set the pace by passing on lower oil prices through the system. Clora and George McAra in Gravenhurst, Ontario entered into a longterm contract with Petro-Canada and put their life savings in a gas station. They attempted to reduce their gas prices in order to be competitive and we saw that Petro-Canada locked their station. The Government oil company is attempting to restrain
March 19, 1986

competition exactly as the big multinational oil companies have done in the past.
I asked the Minister about her policy for Petro-Canada. The Conservative's policy for Petro-Canada is to have it act like any other oil company. That is not why Petro-Canada was established. In my opinion it was established to be a leader. It was established to be a leader in the industry and it has been a leader in the opposite direction in this case.
In the column written by Diane Francis in the Toronto Star, she states:
By my calculation, such a calamitous collapse means gasoline prices should be shaved by about 12 cents a litre.
She stated that last week U.S. posted prices fell to $20 a barrel while Canadian posted prices were as low as $15 a barrel, and by her calculation gasoline prices should be shaved by about 12 cents a litre. She continues:
Instead, we have seen savings of a penny here or there and a great many excuses from Petro-Canada and its rivals.
Why?
"Because there are only four refiners and no competition in Canada", says Ron Greene, president of Renaissance Energy Ltd.
By comparison in the U.S., there are literally hundreds of refiners competing viciously to buy oil, which means the prices often are upwards.
I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will address the Government's policy of expanding Petro-Canada to buy all those gas stations. Why did the Government do that? Do we really want Petro-Canada to own all the gas stations? Or is it more important to have Petro-Canada involved in heavy oil, the tar sands, exploration in the oil upgraders, and so on, which is going to be the real energy future for Canada? I do not want to put down individual retailers, but lots of different people can sell gasoline. Selling gasoline is not in the strategic nature of control of the energy supply. Importing, discovering, participating in some of the frontier resources, becomes strategic. Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary can tell us why the Government has acted this way with Petro-Canada? Again, it has the worst of all possible worlds.
Let me recap. The oil industry is in tatters. The consumer is not getting a break at the pump. Petro-Canada is out of control. So what is the Government doing? In western Canada it is very important to develop future resources. This is very hard to do when oil prices are falling. We have to look ahead to the future because in the 1990s we are going to have another oil shortage. One of our great projects was the Husky upgrader, a proposal entered into between the federal Government and the Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan. The upgrader is at Lloydminster right on the border of Alberta and Saskatchewan. The Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan were to put up a $300 million loan guarantee to Husky, a Canadian private oil company, while Ottawa was to provide a $750 million loan guarantee and a $50 million grant. But the federal Government reneged on its promise.

Across-the-board cuts in provincial royalties or PGRT would be of little benefit to the small to medium-sized independents already paying only 6 per cent royalties and sheltered from PGRT, but would place significiant incremental revenue in the hands of the major companies.

We should consider a negotiated floor price for oil as a temporary situation until the market stabilizes. We should bring forward some real tough competition legislation and kick Petro-Canada and the other big oil companies into passing on those oil prices to consumers at the pumps, because those prices could go

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has expressed some concern, as well he might, about the oil industry in Alberta. I am sure he will recognize that during the past four years when the prices were on the rise the industry in Alberta, had it been healthy, would probably have been able to attain some kind of resource base to endure some of the slump it is now facing. The Hon. Member was in the House at the time the National Energy Program was passed. In fact, I think he may have been his Party's spokesman at the time. His Party was, may I say, widely enthusiastic about the National Energy Program.
I can accept the fact that ideologically, in terms of theory, the Hon. Member at that time would have supported the National Energy Program. He has the benefit of history now and he has seen what that program did to the oil industry, particularly in Alberta and certainly in Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Now that he has seen what that policy did to the industry out west, would he now concede that the National Energy Program was a mistake?
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how many times I have to say this.
One more time.

Okay, I'll say it one more time. The Hon. Member is an honest person. I invite him to check the record. The NDP did not support the National Energy Program. We voted with the Government-rather we voted with-
Oh, oh!

You people, you're the Government now. We voted with the Conservatives just as much as we ever voted with the Liberals.
I rose in the House at the time to say that one of the big flaws in the National Energy Program was that in its effort to get political power for Mr. Trudeau, as opposed to Mr. Lougheed, the Liberal Government shifted the base of exploration from the western sedimentary basin to the frontiers. There were a number of reasons for doing that. First of all, the Government wanted to see what was in the frontiers. I had a plan and I accept some of that. However, the real reason for it was that under the Liberal notion of Canada the federal Government had power over the frontiers. I recall the fights that occurred between Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and the federal Government. A deal was never made with them and the Government said that the offshore belonged to the federal
Government. I thought that that was one of the flaws in the National Energy Program.
Regarding the principles of the National Energy Program, the Conservative Party agreed with its principles as did our Party. We are all for energy security; we are all for fairness to consumers, a viable industry and Canadian ownership. I supported the thrust of Canadianization as did the Conservatives.
I see that the Associate Minister of Defence (Mr. Andre) is present. People used to give him a rough time by saying that he did not believe in Canadianization. He used to rise to point out that that was not true. As energy critic, he did believe in Canadianization, and he was right. An untruth was being told about him. It would be convenient for me to say otherwise, but the truth is that Conservative Members also believed in Canadianization of the oil industry.
Let us tell the truth. The truth regarding the National Energy Program is that I thought that it would not work and that the PIP grants were too expensive and would be abused. The Government spent about $8 billion on PIP grants. For $8 billion we could have bought Imperial Oil. We could have Canadianized the industry instantly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: That would have done a hell of a lot.

Regardless of whether he agrees or disagrees with that, and I suspect he disagrees, my position was that 1 was not in support of the National Energy Program.
Perhaps I can tell this to Hon. Members now since a few years have passed. I had a hell of a struggle within parts of my own Party on the matter of the National Energy Program. With the support of my leader and some other Hon. Members, I got the support I needed. We had people telling us that we had better support Lalonde because he was being attacked by the oil industry. The oil industry went on a capital strike by moving the rigs south and not spending money. Lalonde was being attacked and a group of Canadians led by Robert Laxer and Me! Hurtig supported the National Energy Program. I would not be part of that group because I thought the program was flawed. I invite the Hon. Member to check the record. We did not support the National Energy Program.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to set the record straight. The NDP certainly did favour part of the National Energy Program and that was the 25 per cent back-in whereby Petro-Canada arbitrarily gained one-quarter of offshore acreage.
1 would like to return to the Hon. Member's main point. He said that he would like to see a floor price for crude oil. Would he quickly and succinctly tell me what that price would be?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is right. We did support the 25 per cent back-in. The National Energy Program consisted of 13 Bills and a whole group of programs, some of which Conservative Members supported, but we did not, and some of which we supported and Conservative Members did not. We did support the back-in because we thought for various reasons that it was only fair. After all, the resource
March 19, 1986

did belong to the people and the people were entitled to a chunk of the resource. We did not see any problem with that. It was only the Hon. Member's American friends who browbeat the Government into backtracking on that proposal. In other words, the Government caved in to the Americans on that matter because the Americans did not like their oil companies having to suffer this 25 per cent federal Government back-in.
With respect to an exact price, that price has to be negotiated. It is as simple as that. I invite the Hon. Member to have a look at the Western Accord. There is a provision in Section 9 of the Western Accord that would allow the provincial and federal Governments to get together to negotiate such a price.

Mr. Speaker, now that he has proposed some sort of a price, would the Hon. Member tell us first how it is going to be funded, and second, how it will be organized with the 630,000 barrels a day that are being exported to the United States? The producer will not be selling to that market if he can sell to the Canadian market, and the American market represents three-eighths of our production.

Mr. Speaker, there is a problem with exports. There are ways of getting around that. One is that the producer would sell more to Canadians, but that still would not take care of it all. Another way would be that a deal would be negotiated with the United States. There could be a joint export-import tax that could cover oil so that we would both have the same system. The third way, quite frankly, is to sell oil for export at lower prices. Regarding who would pay for it, it would be a shared cost. The Canadian consumer would in fact be paying part of the burden.
How?

He would be paying higher prices at the pumps, quite honestly. That is not unreasonable. The price at the pumps would still come down since it has not yet come down as far as it should. The consumer would not notice any increase at all at the pumps but would be paying more than he would with a completely free market price.
Is that not what happened under the National Energy Program? The consumer got a break at the pumps at the expense of the Alberta producers. We are interested in fairness, fairness to the consumer and fairness to the producer. That is what Canada is about and that can be done.
The problem is that the Hon. Member has a notion in his head of the great so-called free market which is not a free market at all. It is a crazy world market that is manipulated by the Saudis. I will end by telling the Hon. Member about a public opinion poll that was taken in his own province which shows that there is a substantial minority, almost a majority, of Albertans who would favour such a system.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House this afternoon, to take part in this debate on energy on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney).
The Minister's leadership and ability to negotiate and to appreciate the complexities of this country, are reflected in her truly magnificent record of achievements over the last fifteen months.

The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has by her efforts and patience introduced goodwill into the relationships between provincial and federal Governments. More important, if we are to have the benefits of the jobs which result from investment, she has introduced confidence back into the Canadian energy industry.
The ill-conceived motion now under debate describes the Government's energy policies as disastrous. We have heard that word before. It is a word associated by investors, provincial Governments in Canada and, indeed, the world, with the National Energy Program. The NEP was conceived and inflicted upon Canada by the Liberal Party and the Liberal Government, the very hand which brings us today's motion.
Six years ago we were in the midst of an oil crisis. The Iran-Iraq war in 1979 had severely curtailed production from the Middle East and world prices were escalating. The Government of the day, which has now assumed its rightful role as

March 19, 1986
Supply
the Opposition, was gripped by the kind of hysteria we are hearing from the Liberals today. It reacted in a knee-jerk fashion with a policy which cripped the Canadian oil and gas industry and pitted one region of the country against another. The NEP drove rigs south of the border. It drove away $17 billion in investment. It blackened our reputation in international investment circles. When people said that it was a disaster, they were being too kind. The Liberals have not learned their lesson. They are counselling us to panic again, to adopt politically expedient policies with little thought for the long-term implications for both the industry and consumers in Canada.
What is the situation today? The picture has changed considerably. We are facing a price was in international oil markets, and the oil and gas industry around the world is adjusting to lower prices and to uncertainty. The Canadian must make the same adjustments. Unlike 1980, when it was in the foot by the Liberal Government of the day, it now has under a deregulated regime the flexibility to adjust to market realities. No longer does it face administered prices and overregulation. No longer does it face the uncertainties of federal-provincial energy wrangling. A stable policy framework is in place, supported by a new spirit of federal-provincial reconciliation.
The cornerstones of the new policy environment are the Atlantic Accord, the Western Accord, the agreement on natural gas markets and pricing, and the new frontier energy policies. These new policies were carefully developed in consultation with provincial Governments and with the oil and gas industry. We did not assume that Governments could predict the course of world energy prices. Our goal was to free the industry from excessive regulation and excessive taxation so that it could adjust and compete.
The overwhelming majority of voices from the oil and gas industry demanded relief from the NEP. The message was: "Remove the heavy hand of Government; we are willing to handle the lean times if we can reap rewards when there are good times". In 1985, the first year in which the policies were operational, the Canadian oil and gas industry expressed renewed confidence. The new environment was applauded by the industry, by investors and by observers abroad. An editorial in The Oil and Gas Journal indicated the following: "The Accord does all the right things, which means that it unravels a tangle of wrong things and does so in the right way". Salomon Brothers Inc. indicated: "In contrast to the NEP, the implicit premise of the Western Accord is that the objectives of stimulating investment and job creation in the energy sector and Canada's energy security can best be met by adopting a market-sensitive pricing regime for oil and gas within a fiscal regime of profit-driven taxation".
In response to the new policies, capital investment by the Canadian industry increased from less than $8 billion in 1984 to more than $10 billion in 1985. That year was one of the best in the history of the industry. Well completions in western Canada reached a record high of 11,600, an increase of almost 9 per cent over 1984. Exploration drilling was up by 20 per
cent and development drilling was up by 25 per cent. Natural gas production was up by about 10 per cent and gas exports increased by 25 per cent. The policy framework put in place last year continues to have the confidence of the industry and of the Governments of the producing provinces.
Jim Gray, President of Canadian Hunter, recently told investors in London, England that whatever the price at which oil temporarily settles, "Canada will continue to be well positioned". He pointed out that finding costs for oil in Alberta and Saskatchewan were about half the costs in Oklahoma and Texas.
Imperial Oil President, Arden Haynes, told the same group that "investment in the Canadian oil and gas industry is, once again, a matter of business judgment rather than a political gamble". In other words, the price of oil may be changing, but the oil and gas industry is in a much better position to adapt to these changes than it would have been under the NEP.
Press reports earlier this week indicated that Poco's Petroleums Limited intended to double its capital spending in spite of the decline in oil prices and the resulting decline in the value of the company's assets. The president of the company mentioned increased marketing opportunities for natural gas after deregulation of the industry. He went on to say that Governments should not be encouraged to reregulate crude oil prices, and that "you can't say to a Government, step in when times are tough and stand aside during a boom".
I might add that British Columbia has just signed a new and substantial export sale of natural gas to California. It represents a 10 per cent increase in B.C. natural gas sales this year over last year. This is a direct result of the Western Accord and the new natural gas pricing agreement we reached with the producing provinces last year.
The oilfield service industry is extremely vulnerable to cutbacks spending by producing companies, but I should like to refer to the comments of a leading representative of that industry. Dale Tufts, President of the Petroleum Services Association, said:
We fought long and hard for the Western Accord to reduce Government intrusion and we don'twant to go back to where we were just to save us today.
That position is widely held by the oil and gas industry and is supported by the Governments of the producing provinces. They agree that intervention in response to the oil price decline would be a mistake. John Zaozirny, Alberta's Energy Minister, has called it the worst mistake we could make. Our colleagues in provincial Governments have agreed to keep each other fully informed of developments. The oil and gas industry is important to regional economies.
We are concerned about the impact of falling prices, but we agree it would be a mistake to tinker with public policy based on the experience of three months of unusual trading.
I believe it is appropriate to illustrate just how volatile the oil market is at this time. In the last few days, the spot price has actually gone up. West Texas intermediate is currently
March 19, 1986

trading at $14 a barrel and Brent crude has shown similar price changes, at one point reaching $16 a barrel. Most experts believe that this uncertainty will continue over the short term. That is why it would be foolish to move until the market settles down.
The best solutions for the industry's adjustment to lower crude prices are market led solutions. The changes made by the Government and by the Governments of the producing provinces have given the industry greater flexibility to adopt such solutions.
The ceiling price on so-called old oil has been removed. The petroleum and gas revenue tax is being phased out and has been eliminated on new projects and new productions. On older production it drops from 12 per cent in 1985 to zero in 1988.
Assuming, for purposes of comparison, a crude oil price of $15 a barrel, the net impact of the new policies will be to provide industry with more than $1 billion in cash flow in 1986 over what it would have been under the National Energy Program. That point bears repetition, Mr. Speaker. If the National Energy Program had been left in place and if average crude prices this year were at $15, the cash flow of the Canadian oil and gas industry would be more than $1 billion less than under the new policies.
Adjustments to the uncertainties of oil price changes may be difficult, but they would have been more difficult under the NEP. The new policies have given the industry the fiscal and regulatory room to adjust to changing market conditions best.
The new policies are consistent and stable. But they are non-interventionist and non-discriminatory. They will help the oil and gas industry to do what it can do infinitely better than Governments, that is, adjust to the realities of the market.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, the new policies are helping energy consumers. We have deregulated crude oil. The price of crude oil has dropped, and as the newer, cheaper oil makes its way to refiners the cost of gasoline and heating oil is going down.
Canadian gasoline prices dropped another 2 cents a litre this week. The average total drop in gasoline prices since the first of the year is now 4.3 cents per litre for regular leaded at self-serve stations. In some areas of the country, market competition has seen gasoline prices drop by as much as 11 cents a litre, or about 50 cents a gallon.
The new energy policies are designed to avoid intervention and to allow market forces to set prices. Cheaper average gasoline prices show that the market is working and that our policies are correct.
The new policy also commits us to deregulation of natural gas prices. Industrial natural gas consumers are negotiating prices directly with producers or with distributors under competitive marketing programs. On November 1, 1986, all natural gas prices will be deregulated and all consumers will benefit from competitive gas prices.

In summary, the energy policy of the Government has stood the test. It is consistent with the goals our Party established while in opposition. It fulfils the commitments of the 1984 Prince Albert statement. It has restored confidence in energy investment in Canada. It has provided the oil and gas industry with the fiscal flexibility to deal with the inevitable price cycles of an internationally traded commodity. It has given consumers the benefit of a competitive market. In addition, it has shown that federal and provincial Governments can work together to allow Canadian companies to grow, to adapt and to compete.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister mentioned a price reduction of 4.3 cents a litre, and in some cases, a reduction of as much as 11 cents a litre. Let me say to the Minister that in a few isolated cases where prices have fallen more than 4 cents a litre, it is because of price wars and it has nothing to do with a reduction at the pump.
The Minister mentioned that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has introduced confidence. But the confidence is not there any more. That is why members of the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada and the Canadian Petroleum Association came to Ottawa yesterday to speak to the Minister to ask her what she was going to do. They do not have confidence any more. They do not know where the industry is going. It is a very unfortunate situation.
The Minister mentioned the reduction in the spot price in West Texas intermediate crude. That is not going to matter. Petro-Canada, which does not have much of a source of crude oil itself, was paying, prior to December, the West Texas posted price for crude oil in western Canada. In January, the West Texas spot price went below the West Texas intermediate posted price. Then Petro-Canada decided it would pay the spot price, which was lower than the posted price. If the spot price goes up above the posted price again, Petro-Canada will just offer the producers in western Canada the posted price. Producers will get offered the lower of the two prices, which is the lowest price in the world for crude oil.
This is the country's own Crown corporation. It is supposed to be protecting the industry, securing a supply of crude oil and securing exploration and development, but here it is gouging the producers. How can the Minister defend this action? How can the Minister say that the industry must make adjustments? It is like somebody going into a store and asking for protection money off the top and saying to that storekeeper, "You have to adjust to this". It does not make any sense at all. The Minister is not advocating a responsible position for the industry.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has raised three or four points. First, the variety of prices that have developed with the falling of crude prices is the market-place at work. There will be, and constantly, a pressure on those who sell to find the price that will attract the market-place.
The fact that industry representatives visited here yesterday and will continue to visit, is an indication of the approach my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss

March 19, 1986
Supply
Carney) takes to this process. She consults, she listens and she relates to the provinces. They come to inform. I think you will find, Mr. Speaker, that the natural forces of the market-place are exactly what these people want as a guide, not government intervention.
Finally, with regard to the procedure of Petro-Canada purchasing at spot or medium prices, I would expect that, as an organism which must compete in the market-place, Petro-Canada would look for the best supply and price for its product. It will certainly take 60 days to go through the process from buying to selling. The first proposal of the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) in this House in 1975 was for 45 days, which later changed to 60 days due to a later delay caused by freezing prices, and that was adopted by the Hon. Member's own Party. It is recognized that the material must be processed before it is sold at the pump, but the market-place will determine the final price.

Canadians must wonder what their Governments have done for them. Alberta was like a guy who won a lottery a few years ago. It was getting all that money in its provincial Treasury and it did not really save or invest it properly. Now the whole province is in danger of massive unemployment and shut-downs. The Liberal Government introduced the National Energy Program which did not work, and then retreated from it. It was left with no energy policy at the end of its tenure. The Tory Government has brought in the Western Accord, which the Minister has the gall to tell us is of benefit to the consumer. I cannot see that the consumer or the producer is benefiting. Oil companies are gouging the consumer at one end and the small producer at the other.
Did the Government of Canada take into account that the price of oil was going to decline at the time of the Western Accord? No one complained about the Western Accord because everyone thought the price was going to go down. Did the Government foresee a de-escalation of the world price of oil? What is the Government's policy presently on the big oil industries' desire to get rid of the remaining petroleum and gas revenue tax? Is the Government going to phase that out more rapidly, or has it taken a decision on that yet?

Mr. Speaker, I think Alberta acted very responsibly in recognition of its great resource by building up the funds it did during the period of good times. From all evidence there will be only a very temporary cycle of uncertainty in the pricing of raw materials and the end product.
Oil, gas, and coal are all non-renewable resources. When I was an engineer in the business world, there was a concern that we would not be able to fulfil the industrial and popular requirements for energy from our own resources. There was considerable uncertainty in everyone's mind about the future availability of this natural resource. Because of the surplus in latter years, much of our memory of that has faded. However, when addressing today's issue, we must remember that oil, gas, and coal are non-renewable resources. If we do not increase
the price there will be waste. The entire world, and Canadians in particular, have learned that this is a precious asset. We must use it well, and a firming up of the price is inevitable.

Mr. Speaker, the Member did not answer my question about whether the Government is going to make further changes in the PGRT. Would the Minister not also agree with me that we are seeing no exploration or new projects now and our reserves are not being replaced? In fact, we are now depleting reserves, and the industry cannot be restarted that easily. Has the Minister considered that problem? Will he give me an answer with regard to the PGRT?
Finally, does the Minister really believe that there is a free market in oil, considering what the OPEC countries are doing? That is a cartel. Does the Minister want the cartel to get its act together again? Is there or is there not a free market in oil?

Mr. Speaker, no decision has been taken with regard to changes in the Western Accord or the PGRT. As I announced in my remarks, there is a program in place which will remain in place. With respect to investment in the industry, in my remarks I referred to very specific investments. One organization is doubling its investment because of its confidence in the market-place in the future.
Is there a free market in oil? As I recall, when the oil crisis developed in the early 1970s, OPEC was responsible for the delivery of approximately 60 per cent of the world's oil supply. To the best of my knowledge, that has now decreased to approximately 35 per cent. OPEC does not now have the impact on world prices which it once had. There are other oil resources being developed around the world such as in the North Sea and Nigeria. As a result, mid-eastern oil does not have the effect it once had. I must admit that it is questionable whether this creates a free market in oil.

Mr. Speaker, OPEC does not have the clout it would like to have, but the Saudi Arabians are just playing a waiting game. Before long their clout will be increased quite a bit. The Minister talked about the 40-day and 60-day period before the price of oil would go up. That started in 1973 with the first oil shock when the oil companies wanted to raise the price the next day. They did not talk about a flow-through period at that time. They were not going to wait two months. The Liberal Government of the day said that they must wait 45 days and then 60 days before they could pass that price increase along. That was to protect Canadians against the oil companies. Now that prices are coming down, they say there is this flow-through period. That only shows their own inconsistency.
It's the same thing.
They are waiting voluntarily before reducing the price, but they wanted to raise the price the next day. That 60-day period-

Why does the Minister not just call the President of Petro-Canada and tell him to treat producers fairly, to pay them a fair price for their oil, and to reduce the price at the pumps? My learned friend, the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), quoted an article which said that gasoline prices at the pumps are 12 cents too high. Why does he not tell the President of Petro-Canada to give consumers a break instead of going through this charade of waiting an arbitrary period of time?

Mr. Speaker, all of us in Canada believe there is a place in the market for a large Canadian oil company. However, it has to compete. If we start to establish prices, then obviously we have to supply subsidies right down the line. We have set a goal for Petro-Canada to be a competitor in the market-place. It has to buy and sell in competition with all the others in this field. It is not for this Government to start directing any Crown corporation on the price of its goods and services.
