speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make submissions on the motion moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan). The motion reads as follows:
That this House regrets that the government's energy policy has proven to be disastrous for both the industry and the consumer in its failure to give the consumer the benefit of falling world energy prices and in its confusion and lack of direction, creating uncertainty for the oil and gas industry in the face of the government's inability to cope with changing international conditions and its refusal to fulfill its commitments.
The motion condemns the Government because, in the view of the Opposition and of Canadians in general, this Government has authored the mess which exists in the petroleum industry today. As my colleague pointed out, not only are consumers being gouged by Petro-Canada and the Government, so are the 600 odd small producers.
Supply
I would like to outline very briefly the state of the petroleum industry in Canada at present. It is in trouble. As my colleague pointed out, this Government has no definitive policy to deal with the industry's problems. We all know that the price of crude oil has fallen somewhat dramatically over the last number of months. In fact, as you know, there has been a 52 per cent decline in that price since the end of 1985, and a 57 per cent decline since November 1. As a result, Canadian producers are reducing capital expenditures and laying off employees. We are all aware that in excess of 25,000 jobs are threatened by the confused state of the energy sector. This Conservative Government has to take some responsibility for its inaction and hands-off policy in this regard.
As you know, Syncrude recently cut $200 million from its planned expenditures for 1986. Roxy Petroleum is reducing staff and has cut its capital spending in half. Syncrude and Suncor have announced lay-offs at their projects in Fort McMurray, Alberta. Texaco will also cut its experimental heavy oil project at Fort McMurray and put 200 Canadians out of work. Husky Oil will lay off 300 employees by the end of March, 1986. The Calgary Herald of March 12 announced that Petro-Canada has laid off about 300 staff members. Other Canadian producers, including Sulpetro and Sceptre Resources, have also indicated they will soon be cutting their employee rosters. On March 14, Dome Petroleum Limited announced that it had asked its creditors to forgo principal and interest payments of as much as $1 billion on its total longterm debt of $6 billion. The facts speak for themselves. The industry is in trouble.
What, pray tell, is this Government doing in order to assist the industry? The Minister stands up and, with her usual pomposity, says that the industry will take care of itself. As a result of deregulation everything will be hunky-dory in the months and years to come. The Minister, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) are conning Canadians when they say that it will take time, one has to take flow-through into consideration. We on this side refer to that as the flow-through excuse. As my colleague indicated, it is an excuse for the major oil companies to rip off consumers. That is the bottom line. The consumers, those who have to go to the gas stations once or twice a week, are being ripped off, no question about it. We in the Opposition, in particular our energy critic, have led the fight for consumers in Canada. Our energy critic has pointed out time and time again that Canadians are paying an unconscionable price for gasoline in view of the world price of oil. Yet the Government just throws up its hands and says it takes time for the cheaper oil to work its way through the system.
At first blush one could possibly conclude there might be some merit to that argument. There is a delay from the time contracts are entered into and the oil is delivered and refined and works its way to the pumps. At first blush that might make some sense. However, if that were the case, then why do our friends in the U.S. pay so much less for gasoline? Why does a motorist in Buffalo pay anywhere up to 15 cents a litre less than a motorist in Toronto? It does not make any sense.

March 19, 1986
Supply
Where is the fairness? Where is the equity? Where is the justice? Surely if the flow-through excuse has some merit, then the same thing would apply to our friends south of the border. Yet it does not. So we say it is an excuse used by the oil companies to continue ripping off the consumer. As was pointed out by my colleague, when the price of oil went up the multinationals put the price of gasoline up immediately. When the Government of the day argued that it takes time to work its way through the system, the oil companies said no, they have to put the price up right away. In effect, the consumer is getting hit at both ends. When the price of crude oil goes up, the multinationals want to put the price of gasoline up almost immediately. When it comes down they say it takes time to work its way through the system. Neither I nor the Liberal Party believe that this Government recognizes the gravity of the problem in the oil industry.
Let me speak once again about the jobs which are at risk because of the Government's inaction. We can understand why the Government does not want to take any action. As the Hon. Member from North Bay indicated, it is a so-called free enterprise Government. Its motto is to deregulate and get its hands off the business of the nation. It advocates letting business regulate itself.
I have to laugh, as do a great many other people, when our friends opposite talk about free enterprise. It seems to me that when it is convenient to speak of free enterprise then, indeed, Members opposite speak of it. Hon. Members might recall seeing a few years ago full-page advertisements in the major newspapers of Canada depicting a dove in a cage. The caption read: "Let's free enterprise". It was a national advertising campaign paid for by the major corporations of Canada. They felt that some enterprise was not free. Some of the contributors to that campaign, some of the very people who argued for free enterprise, were the same companies to come to the Government cap in hand when they were in desperate need of Government support. I wonder whether the Canadian Commercial Bank, the Northland Bank, Massey-Ferguson or other corporations which have come to the Government cap-in-hand believed that when times are good we should "free" enterprise.
I wonder whether they contributed to that national advertising campaign.
The point I am making is that the oil industry, when it is convenient, says to the Government of Canada: "Leave us alone. We don't want you or need you". However, when times are tough the industry is prepared to go to the Government cap in hand looking for assistance.
There are those who argue that there should be a floor price for crude oil. The Conservative Government of Canada is an accessory to the great Canadian oil rip-off being perpetrated by the oil multinationals. It is within the jurisdiction of the Government to take action in order to reduce the price of gasoline. It is a simple matter. Each and every one of us in the House-each and every Canadian-is a shareholder in a major oil company. We own that company and it is ripping us
off when we go to the pumps. Canadians are asking why we have a national oil company. Surely we do not have such a company for it to be a party to a rip-off, an accessory to the greatest oil gouge in Canadian history. That is a breach of trust and a breach of faith. There is certainly a conflict here. Mr. Hopper sits in his ivory tower, wherever it is-presumably in western Canada-earning his in excess of $400,000 per year. He is saying to the people of Canada that, even though it is our oil company, Petro-Canada is not prepared to take action to assist the consumers. As Hon. Members know, Petro-Canada owns a great many gasoline stations in Canada. In fact, in Ontario, the province where I reside, one in three gasoline stations is owned by Petro-Canada.
Given the position this company holds in the petroleum industry in Canada it is in position to direct a downward spiral with regard to the price of gasoline. It has refused to do so because of a lack of direction, I suppose from the Government, or perhaps because it is receiving the wrong type of direction from the Government. The Government has said to Petro-Canada: "Maximize profit. Run your business like any other. Do what you have to do in order to make a profit". Normally speaking, a company has a duty to its shareholders to maximize profits. That is the bottom line in the private sector. If private sector companies do not maximize profits then they should not be in business. In my view, the bottom line for Petro-Canada is not only to show a profit. We shareholders are asking for more. Of course we would like this Crown corporation to do well. However, we are not simply asking for a profit at the end of the road or at the end of the fiscal year. We want to know that Petro-Canada has been used as a vehicle to further public policy in keeping with the best interests of Canada and Canadians. That is not the role that Petro-Canada is playing.
In days gone by when I had to fill up my gas tank I would make en effort to fill up at Petro-Canada. I had a feeling of pride. I had a feeling that this was our national oil company. Somehow I felt good about Filling up at Petro-Canada. I am losing that feeling.
Good!

I am losing that feeling because of the insensitivity of Petro-Canada. I am certain that a great many Canadians no longer feel proud about the role it plays because of this Government's policies. We know what the Government has in mind for Petro-Canada. We know that some six or seven years ago the Conservative Government under its former Leader decided to govern as if it had a majority. Back then it tried to indicate to Canadians that it wanted to privatize Petro-Canada. We know what happened to that Government when it mismanaged the energy industry. It said to Canadians that, notwithstanding the nature of its mandate, it was going to bulldoze through a substantial increase in the price of gasoline. Here we are seven years later and the Government has still not learned its lesson. It is still bent on privatizing Petro-Canada. It still refuses to allow it to take the lead in reducing the price of gasoline.
March 19, 1986

In his speech the Minister indicated that there have been some price declines in the cost of gasoline. He indicated an amount of four cents. I would have appreciated an opportunity to ask the Minister what he believes to be a fair decrease in the price of gasoline. In this respect it must be kept in mind that the price of crude oil is below $15 a barrel.
I have had the pleasure of knowing the Minister's son for a number of years. He is an alderman on Toronto City Council. He is a very progressive and forward-looking individual. The next time I speak to Jack I will have to ask him where he went wrong with respect to his father and the policies which he supports. Yes, the Minister's son, Jack, is a member of City Council in Toronto and a member of the NDP caucus on City Council. He believes, as we believe on this side of the House, that the Government's policies and those espoused by his father who represents the Government of Canada are wrong and that the people of Canada are being ripped off.
I note that you are indicating my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I had much more to say with respect to how the Government is mismanaging the oil industry, but I look forward to questions from Members opposite. I know that many of them will want to ask me a question on this very important subject.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very intently to the Hon. Member's remarks. Does the Hon. Member recall December, 1979, as well as I do? I remember filling up my gas tank in this city on the day after the Liberal Opposition at the time defeated a very forward looking Conservative Government. The price of gasoline was $1.06 per gallon.
When the Liberal Government left office in the summer of 1984, the price of gasoline was approximately 50 cents a litre or $2.50 a gallon.
There has been a 10 per cent drop, which is 4 cents per litre or about 20 cents per gallon, while the price of gasoline under the previous Liberal Government, of which his colleagues were a part, rose by over a dollar a gallon in most parts of Canada. Would he comment on that discrepancy and indicate why he is so negative about the fact that gasoline prices have dropped at least 10 per cent under the present administration?

Canadians know that they are being ripped off today because of the Government and its policies. The Minister chuckles, but he knows that in January alone, Canadians paid over $300 million too much for gasoline. He knows that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Based on what? Where did you get your figures?

They have woken up across the way. The Parliamentary Secretary asks me where I get my figures. I would be pleased to share the figures with him.
The Petroleum Marketers Association of Canada have put in considerable research to conclude that "Canadian consumers overpaid $302 million in January, 1986, for gasoline". If he
Supply
wants to dispute the position taken by the Petroleum Marketers Association, I suggest he do so.
However, getting back to the Minister, he knows, and his constituents and his colleagues know, that the price of gasoline in Canada today should be at least 10 cents a litre less than it is at the pumps. He knows that because the price of crude oil is less than $15 a barrel and should result in a further decrease of at least 10 cents a litre for the Canadian consumers.

Does the Hon. Member not realize that what Canadians are paying for today is the tremendous burden of deficit which resulted from the National Energy Program and retrograde policy of the Government of which his colleagues were members?
He has not yet answered my question. The price of gasoline in Canada in December, 1979, was approximately 25 cents a litre. When the Liberal Government left office, the price of gasoline virtually doubled to about 50 cents a litre. It has dropped by an average of 4 cents a litre or 20 cents a gallon. Why does he not acknowledge that it was under the Liberals that this great burden of deficit and gasoline taxes were levied on all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, the Minister claims to be a reasonably intelligent person. It seems to me that he is trying to con the House and the people of Canada.
He knows that the factors are different now. We were not dealing with a price of crude oil at $ 15 or $ 12 a barrel.
That is not the reason.

May I take this opportunity to comment on how the Government finds it very convenient to look to the Liberal record and blame it on the Liberals when everything goes wrong? If it rains or snows, blame it on the Liberals. If the sun shines, interest rates go down or unemployment goes down, it is because of Brian and the good policies of the Conservative Government.
Canadians are not so dumb as to believe that. If anything, the Government underestimates the intelligence of the average Canadian. Is it any wonder that the Conservative Government has frittered away that massive mandate it received on September 4? Is it any wonder that the Conservative Government is now trailing in popular support?
You still did not answer my question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend, the Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) for bringing this motion forward. It gives us an opportunity to clear up some of the inaccuracies that have been cast about by the Opposition this afternoon and to truly participate in what I consider to be a very legitimate debate in the House.

March 19, 1986
Supply
Of course, Canada is energy. Energy is the vast resources that this country has at its disposal. Energy is the millions of Canadians working to put the country back on a sound economic footing after the erosion of our economy by the previous Government.
I want to dwell on some of the comments made this afternoon by my friend, the energy critic for the Liberal Party. I believe that they were somewhat unfair and should be corrected for the record.
He said that the flow-through process was a con. He is nodding in agreement. I asked him earlier if the flow-through process was a con when oil prices were rising and the Liberal Government enforced a 60-day freeze before higher prices were permitted at the pumps. I do not understand why it was not a con then but it is today.
Let me quote from Hansard of June 23, 1975, at page 7031 when the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), the Minister of Finance at that time, said:
Against this background I would like to announce on behalf of the government and my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, that on July I this year the price of crude oil and its equivalents will rise by $1.50 per barrel to $8 per barrel. We are again asking industry to refrain from reflecting this increase in their product prices until 45 days have passed. By that time-
I want the Hon. Member to listen to this carefully:
-inventories held at the former crude oil price will, on average, have been used up.
Later he increased that to a 60-day period because he was convinced, after examination, that it took 60 days for it to flow through the system.
The Hon. Member stands up in the House with his selfrighteous attitude to say that it was only on behalf of consumers that they arrived at that figure. That is not accurate. For him to stand up today and say that the flow-through is a con is not really to tell the truth. I wanted to correct that and I think the Hon. Member will agree with me that it is not really a con but in fact reflects what is really happening.
A drop of 2 cents a litre is equivalent to approximately $4 a barrel, in round figures, or a decrease of about 0.5 cents a litre per dollar. So what we see now are two drops in the price of gasoline, it has dropped 4.3 cents a litre so far, which reflects a drop of a little over $8 a barrel. If we are talking about the flow-through period, which we are, the average posted price at the end of December was $27.42 U.S. At the end of January, it was $24.32 U.S., which is a drop of $3 a barrel on average. The big crunch came in February, as we all know. The average February posted price was $16.78 U.S. If we go through March and into April, we can see we have every right to expect further decreases in gasoline prices at the pumps beginning early in April, at least, to my estimation. The average posted price now for the first two weeks of March is $12.44 U.S., which will be reflected further on down the road as the flow-through goes through.
The Hon. Member must be fair with the Canadian public. I understand what the Opposition is doing. It is making a big
political ploy out of this issue and creating confusion in the minds of the public. When the public sees in the media that the price of a barrel of oil has dropped, they feel it should, therefore, drop at the pump tomorrow. I understand that. But I believe the Hon. Member, who has been the energy critic for the Opposition for a while, understands, and behind that tough-talking facade he presents to the House of Commons, he knows full well how the system operates. He has spent enough time with Husky-Bow Valley lately to know its corporate plans intimately by this time. He knows the system and how it works, that the domestic crude moving through the pipeline takes a three to four-week period and that the inventory of crude at the refinery is kept there for a week. The refining of crude, the blending of gasoline, storage and distribution take another six weeks before it gets to the retailer. That works out to about 60 days.
I believe the Canadian public should understand this. All I am saying to the Hon. Member is that I understand why he is making a political ploy out of this issue. It is great stuff to talk about the great rip-offs and everything else.
We talked not too long ago about the margins, the return on investment which the downstream operations were receiving, and the Hon. Member himself admitted that it was not spectacular over the last three or four years. So I would question this "great rip-off' that so many people talk about.
I just returned from the United States. Normally when I go on holidays or on a trip, the first thing 1 look at is the price of gas at the pumps, no matter where I am in the world. In the United States, Americans complained to me that the price of gas was not coming down fast enough for them either. The Hon. Member said today that as soon as prices dropped, the prices in the United States dropped at the pump. That is just not so. It has not shown up in any of the information, nor has it been indicated at the pumps that way. Companies in the United States are also using up inventories. They have the flow-through process to contend with, although I will say to the Hon. Member, to those watching the televised debate and to those Hon. Members in the House, that the American flow-through is a much quicker process than ours. There is no question about that. It is because of volumes and economy of scale. It is a shorter period, but there is still a flow-through period. We talk about a variation in prices. As of the very latest statistics we have, there is a differential of 13 cents a litre, after taking the American dollar and U.S. gallon into consideration, most of which we can chalk up to taxes-not all, but most of it.
A friend of mine who took the trip with me to the United States hurt his finger. He dislocated his knuckle. He had to go to a clinic to get it fixed. He was there ten minutes. He had it straightened out, splinted, and then had to pull out his plastic to pay the $150 bill. Had he bought the supplementary health plan for travellers outside of this country, he would have been covered. Had he been an American and had he not had a private plan, he would not have been covered. But a Canadian in Canada would have been covered. We have services here in Canada which have to be paid for. That is part of spreading
March 19, 1986

the tax burden as widely as we can. Part of that tax burden is on gasoline. Yes, our prices are higher.
1 mentioned the economy of scale. There are so many more people in the United States, its refineries are larger because of the economy of scale, and so on, and it can produce the product at a much more competitive rate. That is the difference. I believe we should be honest with the Canadian people. They must understand that we are concerned about what is going on in the energy field today, naturally, and we are watching the situation very carefully.
Some comments were made that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) was not concerned or involved. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that she has met with government officials and the Energy Ministers in the producing provinces, especially in Alberta where the problem looms the largest. She has met with the producers, not only the Canadian Petroleum Association but the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, made up of Canadian producers, and I can tell you right now, Mr. Speaker, that these people are keeping her informed on a daily basis as to what is going on in the oil patch and the problems they are experiencing now or will experience over a prolonged period of time. At the same time, however, they are not asking for Government intervention. They do not want the Government to step in and set a floor price, as the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys suggested. Our friends from the New Democratic Party, the socialists, as usual, are at it again; interfere, intervene, dictate, tell them what to do.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said so many things today. He said we should bring in a floor price, negotiate a floor price. First, no one wants to negotiate a floor price. The producing provinces do not want to negotiate a floor price right now. The producers do not want to have one thrust on them. So who do we negotiate with? Second, the Hon. Member says we cannot negotiate right now, anyway, because the situation is too volatile. He says to wait until things settle down. That was his next argument. Then, towards the end of his speech, he said to my colleague from Calgary that we had better have a floor price right now. He was all over the map, which is typical of the New Democratic Party. It does not know where it stands on this thing.
If we set artifically high oil prices-and that is what we are doing if we establish a floor, and the world prices go before that, all of a sudden our manufacturers become uncompetitive, energy intensive industries are penalized, we have lost jobs across Canada and our exports do not look quite as attractive to the United States, for example, where over 600,000 barrels of oil go every day, especially our heavy oil. Now is not the time to panic. It is not the time for any major reactions on what is going on in the industry.
Yesterday, on the strength of the OPEC meetings, the spot price went up $1.25, and today, I understand, it is up $1.45 again. That is on the strength of what is going on there. Tomorrow, those talks could collapse and that approximate $2.50 could disappear. For the Government to step in now and dictate a floor price would be rather ludicrous.
Supply
1 heard the Hon. Member say that we are paying an outrageous price for energy in this country. As a matter of fact, we have very highly competitive energy prices. The Hon. Member ought to travel to Europe and see what Britain, France, Germany and Norway are paying for gas at the pumps. All of a sudden, Canada would look pretty good.
I was pleased to learn today that tourism from the United States and Canada was up by 18 per cent in January. I think that bodes well for the tourism industry in 1986. I think there will be mammoth increases in tourism this year, not only because of Expo 86, that great show that will be held in Vancouver.
The theme of Expo 86 is transportation, and my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), will be playing a key role in welcoming people from around the world to beautiful downtown Vancouver this summer. Vancouver Centre, as a matter of fact, is the riding of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and I am sure she will also be playing hostess to many people from around the world. I am sure she would want me to encourage the these people to come.
The price of gasoline is not discouraging tourism in Canada. If that were the case, we would see the tourism records falling rather than increasing. I think a lot of that credit has to go to the Minister of Tourism (Mr. Murta) for the excellent marketing job he has been doing in the United States. Let me say to those Americans who may be beamed in, we welcome you here with open arms.
Just for a moment, I would like to review what has happened in the 19 months since the overwhelming victory of this Government. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources set in place what is today a world-respected energy policy. It is a policy that puts Canada in a better position than any other country in the world.
I spent a considerable amount of time speaking to people from the energy sector. I was not speaking to representatives of the multinationals but to Canadian geologists, those fellows who have the expertise and are respected and work around the world. I spoke to the drillers, those fellows who do the tough and dirty work, and I spoke to the suppliers. Do you know what they told me? They told me that the new policy is magnificent and allows them the freedom to explore and to work. They are poised to go ahead.
Last year was a record year for the energy sector. It was a record year because of the new energy policy and because of the confidence they have in the Government and its policies. We saw record drilling and record finds last year. The energy industry took off. Certainly there are some concerns now because of falling prices, but if we were under an administrated price system at this time, there would be disaster in the industry because of all those taxes, the taxes that were removed once we got rid of the National Energy Program. Had those taxes still been in place, we would have seen a major disaster within the energy sector.

March 19, 1986
Supply
We signed the Atlantic Accord. The people from Newfoundland wanted to be equal partners in Confederation and they feel that they are now. In fact, Mobil Oil Canada plans to invest $4.2 billion in the Hibernia oil field off the coast of Newfoundland. That will create more than 14,000 person-years of employment in Canada of which more than 9,500 will be in Newfoundland and Labrador. The Atlantic Accord is going in the right direction and it has been applauded widely by all concerned.
Then we had the Western Accord. That set in place the freedom of an industry to do the job it is supposed to be doing and not to be fettered by all these weird taxes, regulations and PIP grants. Canada's oil industry is freed of all those excessive regulations and unfair taxes. As a matter of fact, the reaction in Calgary, as I know my friend, the Hon. Member for Calgary North (Mr. Gagnon), will agree, was to celebrate. They were dancing in the streets. The oil and gas industry rejoiced because finally the market-place was back in vogue. That was most important. The Western Accord was a victory for all Canadians, though, not just for Calgarians and Edmontonians. It was a victory for the manufacturing sector in Ontario and Quebec.
I can say right now that Canadians are benefiting from the lower oil prices, and they will benefit further, there is no question about it. The recent study done by the Conference Board showed that an oil price drop to $18 U.S. would add about .2 per cent to the level of the real GNP in 1986 and .9 per cent in 1987. I suppose there are winners and losers in the province. I think that we will find in the short run that we will have some problems with falling prices, but in the long run they will recover and they will recover in the not too distant future. I do not think prices will skyrocket out of sight. Under the National Energy Program, prices today would have been $39 per barrel.
The Government's energy policy has set the industry free to do what it does best, respond to the challenges and opportunities provided by the market-place in the best interests of all Canadians. Consumers are benefiting from lower world energy prices. The petroleum industry and provincial Governments are content with the progressive energy policies now in place in Canada. The industry is prepared to weather the current market conditions as long as it is left alone to reap the benefits when the market trends reverse.
The Government has fulfilled the commitments it made to Canadian consumers and the petroleum industry. To say that the policy is in a shambles is not right because the consumers were always at the front of our policies when we discussed them. Canada now has a flexible and fair energy policy, one of the most attractive and internationally competitive in the world. The only confusion about that fact rests with the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose we will have to put the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary down as being doubtful in his support for this motion. With all due respect, I do not think that January is a good month in which to measure tourism. I do not think that there are a great many people who travel to
Canada by car during the month of January. I believe the summer will tell the story, and if the summer season indicates that there is an increase in tourism, then certainly the Hon. Member will have a point.
1 do not see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) as being concerned. I would have hoped that she would be here today to discuss this very important question. The motion before us is a comprehensive one and it really needs to be debated. I think her presence here was warranted.
The Parliamentary Secretary says that there is a shorter flow-through period in the United States and that that is the reason the price was able to decline more quickly. 1 do not agree. Eighty per cent of Canada's oil is supplied within Canada. We use about 1.4 million barrels per day and about
1.1	million barrels per day are produced here in Canada. There is quite a short flow-through period, certainly not justifying the two months that the Government says is necessary.
The Parliamentary Secretary referred to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and said that when he was Minister of Finance, he imposed a 45-day period before an increase in the price of gasoline. We must look at the fact that the industry wanted to increase the price the next day when world crude oil prices rose. At that time the Government said that there would be a transition period, that prices would not rise for a certain period of time in case it was an interim increase. It did not want consumers affected that way. I think it was a fair decision. Now, when prices go down, the industry wants to delay. We are still not sure what benefit the industry will give to the consumer or whether the consumer will receive the full benefit of the decline in world oil prices.
It is not a question of flow-through. As I said earlier, in the United States prices went down because retail gasoline is a separate commodity from crude oil, just as crude oil is a separate commodity from pork bellies. It does not relate to a flow-through period; it relates to the fact that there is a competitive situation and true deregulation in the United States. There is no deregulation in Canada when there are a few refineries, and particularly a Crown corporation, holding up the Canadian public and sticking a knife in the back of producers in terms of what it is offering. We are getting the worst of both worlds.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for jogging my memory on a couple of matters which I meant to mention in my remarks but did not. He can correct me if I am wrong, but I believe he said that there were four refineries in Canada.
No, I never said that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Well, somebody said it.

Four major ones.
March 19, 1986

Mir. McDermid: 1 can name about 10-Turbo, Chevron, Co-op, Petrosar, Ultramar, Irving, Shell, Texaco, Petro-Canada, Esso and Suncor; they all have refineries in Canada. As I understand it, there can be fair competition, and I think there is a fair number of them.
I was interested in the comments of the Hon. Member when he talked about Petro-Canada earlier today. I am not exactly sure now where the Liberals stand; it is very confusing. They want Petro-Canada to lead the price down but, when the price rises, they do not want it to lead the price up. They want us to call the President of the company and tell him what to do and how to run his company. If that is the case, why does it not just become a Department or part of the Ministry of Energy and let the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources run Petro-Canada? We are not sure if they think it is too big now, if that was not intended in the first place, if we should sell it to the public or hang on to it. They are all over the map.
We must remember what was done by the Liberals, in conjunction with their NDP friends, in the minority Government of 1972-74. As one of the conditions of the Liberals maintaining their power in that period of time, they sold out their soul to their NDP friends to establish Petro-Canada, a window on the oil industry for exploration, to find out what was going on. What happened next? Then we find that it was into downstream activities by obtaining BP, Petrofina and so on, for which it paid exorbitant rates, according to any analyst.
It was kind of like the Sun Oil purchase.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I disagreed with that one too. My hon. friend across the way has referred to the Ontario Government purchase of Sun Oil. I was not pleased with that decision. I still have not had it explained to me properly, either. In any event, Petro-Canada is now a major oil company with upstream and downstream operations. We are not sure where the Liberals stand. We know what the NDP wants.
Lower prices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: The NDP wants to keep Petro-Canada and it wants to buy Imperial Oil. That is the first thing on its shopping list if and when it gets into power, heaven forbid!
That is not the first thing. What are you talking about?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The other day the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) said that Canada was the toughest country in the world to govern and that if it were easy, we would turn it over to the NDP to run. He was absolutely right. We know exactly where NDP Members stand, but we are not sure where the Liberals stand.
At the present time the Government is examining ways to maintain a Canadian presence and ownership in the oil industry and at the same time rid ourselves, "ourselves" being the Government, of what has grown into an oil company. It is just another oil company. I think it was the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) who said that he did not like
Supply
going in there to fill up any more, so we know how he feels about Petro-Canada.

Mr. Speaker, would the Hon. Member care to explain from where he gets his information? He makes compelling arguments based on what now would appear to be information drawn out of a hat. From where did he get the information that the first thing the NDP would do, when it formed the Government, is to take over Imperial Oil?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member checks with his energy critic-
I am asking from where the Hon. Member got the information.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I was about to say that if the Hon. Member checked with his energy critic, he would find out from where I got the information. He felt that we should be taking over more foreign companies in the energy industry and, in his words, "our first target would probably be Imperial Oil".
That is a different thing altogether.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to tell the Parliamentary Secretary exactly what is the policy of the Liberal Party on Petro-Canada. I think it is well known that we do not object to Petro-Canada being a vehicle of public policy. We feel that the Government should be able to direct Petro-Canada in its actions and act on behalf of consumers and producers. We are totally against the sale of any of the shares of Petro-Canada. When we said we wanted Petro-Canada to be a window on the market-place, we did not mean a whole hothouse. The purchase of Petrofina was to give its stations a presence in eastern Canada. The purchase of Gulf Canada is redundant because the window on the market-place was there. As I said, we now have a whole hothouse on the market-place. There is no competition because of the size of Petro-Canada and because of the Government's policy of gouging the producer and the consumer to try to boost the profit picture of Petro-Canada to make the best possible presentation in the market-place of an issue of shares to the private sector. It is ridiculous.
Canadians do not like Petro-Canada because of what the Government has done to it. Petro-Canada as a Crown corporation is perfectly acceptable and desirable to the Canadian public. However, Canadians do not want their own Crown corporation turned against them and gouging them, as the Government is doing in a cowardly fashion. Telling Petro-Canada to gouge consumers and producers, and then running, hiding and letting on that it had nothing to do with it, is not only bad economic policy or treachery to Canadians, but is downright cowardice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it interesting that when the Liberals were in power and the prices of Petro-Canada were the same or higher than those of most other stations, it was not considered to be gouging the population then. Now, because the Conservatrices are in power and its prices are the

same as its competitors' in the market-place, it is gouging the public. The Hon. Member cannot have it both ways. I, for one, do not believe that the Canadian public is that stupid.
He agrees with that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Sure he does; he is nodding his head and smiling.
I am not agreeing with that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The Canadian public does not buy that. The Canadian public has come to realize that Petro-Canada has been, always was and will be just another oil company. The Liberal Government had a window on the oil industry. It knew what was going on. It taxed that industry. It knew its inner workings, how it operated and everything else. I, for one, do not understand why they ever brough in Petro-Canada in the first place back in 1972-74. I do not think it has served a useful purpose. I think the Canadian people are beginning to realize that.
I am for Canadianization. I am all for Canadian ownership and I am all for Canadian companies, but I like them to be owned by the Canadian people, in the private sector and not by the Government. I have done a tremendous amount of travelling in the last year in some countries where the Government owns everything. It is a disaster. I do not think that the Government should be in the oil industry peddling gas up and down the streets.

Mr. Speaker, I will have to be brief given that there are only nine minutes left. I say to my colleague to whom I indicated that I would leave a few moments for him, that it may be a few moments because I had not realized at the time that I would have only nine minutes. In any event, let me try to be as brief as I can.
I have for years felt that there was a singular lack of competition within the oil industry at the retail level. I have raised this matter not only here in the House of Commons but I can recall asking for an inquiry some years ago when I served in the Ontario Legislature. It was clear to me that it could not simply be by accident that every single gas station in any one area would charge exactly the same price for all of its products.
It was clear to me that if there was any competition of any kind that competition was solely the result of the effort of the gas station operator and his or her ability to provide a higher level of service and not a cheaper product.
I felt, I think probably now over 25 years, that some kind of action should be taken to bring about a competitive situation within the retail end of the petroleum industry here in Canada.
I can remember, at the time when the now Minister of Energy, Mines and Ressources (Miss Carney) introduced the Western Accord, she said:
Since the national energy policy was imposed ... Canadians have suffered from a bureaucratic nightmare, a nightmare which has frightened away foreign
investment, boosted prices at the pumps, and discouraged those who wanted to go out and find new sources of oil and gas. Those days arc over, too... We arc going to create the environment for market forces to operate with buyers and sellers involved. If prices go down, the product prices should go down.
This was the Minister's line at the time on March 28, 1985, when she brought to the House of Commons with great fanfare the Western Accord that she had been able to sign.
I must say that anyone looking at the events of the last few months within the oil industry would have to come to the conclusion that notwithstanding the intent of the Minister- and I do not for one moment doubt that she was serious and sincere in what she said-the result has been quite different.
We have not seen the kinds of reductions at the pump that ought to have been reflected as a result of the dramatic drop in world oil prices. We have, in fact, seen the continuation of managed prices, prices dictated by the major oil companies. We have seen the attempts being made on a continuous basis to strangle any of the independents who dared to step out of line. We have had examples of people and families who were in the retail oil business and who wanted to sell their product in a competitive market-place at a price that would have been somewhat below that charged by the major outlets, only to discover that they were either refused delivery of the product by those from whom they must purchase or they were told directly where there was any kind of contractual arrangement that they could not under any circumstances set a price that would, in their judgment, undercut or undermine the major outlets which were located in the immediate or same area as the independent operation.
Quite frankly, I say to the Minister of Energy, in her absence but through the Parliamentary Secretary, that even with the best intentions in the world, the structure that we have in Canada for the distribution of petroleum products to the consumer is managed in such a way as to make it virtually impossible for the competitive market-place, about which the Minister and her colleague speak so highly, to operate effectively, if at all. It is toward that end that we must address ourselves.
The Minister made much on the twelfth of this month of an announcement by Imperial Oil and Petro-Canada that they were going to reduce the price of gasoline by 2 cents per litre. The problem with it is that any reasonable thinking individual would have to agree that a reduction of 2 cents a litre, given the dramatic drop in the price of oil is miniscule. The drop from almost $30 a barrel to $12 a barrel should out of necessity result in something considerably more than a 2 cents a litre benefit to the consumer.
It not only is not enough, Mr. Speaker, there were areas in the country that did not even get the benefit of the 2 cents a litre drop.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Where?

In Toronto. Yes, where there had been one of those fictitious price wars going on, one of those drops in the price that are the result of the back-up of petroleum in the

system and the necessity to move it more quickly through the system.
That is not fictitious.
It was not a price war in the sense that you and I understand it.
A back up.

It was because there was a back up in the system and ail of the majors decided to move it through the system more quickly that they had to reduce the price. That is all. It was nothing to do with the price war. It was a managed price again.
If it was necessary to do that, then clearly it was done for one set of reasons, entirely separate and apart from the dramatic drop in the world price of oil, and everyone in Canada should benefit from the actual reduction of cost to the oil companies themselves and should benefit from the reduction of world price.
I did promise my colleague a few moments. I am sorry it is only two minutes, but I yield the floor to my colleague in the Conservative Party.

election. I find him a real gentleman, a parliamentarian and one of the few who can logically develop an argument and articulate it. We have seen a good example of it. He talked about competition, and certainly we need more competition in the market-place.
One thing we, as the Government, have done is to remove any barriers for the transportation of petroleum and petroleum products across borders. This allows the independent dealers to import those gasoline products and not be locked in to the major refiners.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) talked about the need to change the PGRT tax credit. He has analysed that very well. It is something that has to be done, but I must emphasize that it is only 57 days since the price collapsed. It is premature to act at this time. One only has to look at the spot market for the last three days. Prices have been going up. To act now is too soon.
